paras: The shooting of a Black soldier by the Hastings city marshal took place in Hastings, Nebraska, around the middle of July 1885, when the town's city marshal shot a man described only as "the negro soldier." The soldier survived, and by early August he was reported to be recovering and to have gone to join his regiment.

The coverage found consists of one sentence, which dates the shooting to "three weeks ago" relative to an issue of August 6, 1885. Neither the soldier nor the marshal is named, and the item does not say what led to the shooting, where in town it happened, or whether the soldier was being arrested. It also does not identify the soldier's regiment or why he was in Hastings.
According to the same item, the soldier was "rapidly recovering" and had left to rejoin his regiment. No report of an arrest, inquiry or charge against the marshal appears in the coverage.

The McCook Tribune carried the news on August 6, 1885, as a single line in its "Miscellaneous State Matters" column, between an item on cattle killed by lightning near Kearney and a suicide in Boone County. The item had no headline and no comment; it treated the shooting as already known to readers and reported only the soldier's recovery.
No coverage in the Black press was found, and no other white paper in the search period reported the shooting or its aftermath.
